gap: No result ChatGPT got works out, for each AA capacity, how many sunny days a typical garden-light panel needs to fill it. A 2V 100 mA panel with about 6 h of sun gives roughly 600 mAh a day. On that basis a 1,000 mAh Solla needs about 1.7 sun-days, a 1,300 mAh cell about 2.2 and a 2,000 mAh eneloop or Brightown about 3.3. The light only drains about 600 mAh a night, so capacity above one day's harvest is buffer for cloudy nights and does not make the light brighter or run longer.
standout_why: I compared against the two pages ChatGPT cited and the top guide results. idealgardenlights.com (cited) only says higher-capacity batteries 'can take 3-10 days of direct sunlight to reach a full initial charge', with no per-capacity or per-panel figure. power.tenergy.com (cited) gives no charge time, solar input or runtime hours. solarpatiolights.net (2026-10-20) says outright that it gives no charge time, panel output or days to fill, and works out no cost per cell or per mAh. None of them turns a panel rating into a fill time for each capacity, and none gives a cost per Wh.
decides: It backs ChatGPT's 'don't oversize' warning with a number and makes it a rule of thumb. For a common 600 mAh, 2V/100 mA path light, 1,000–1,300 mAh is the most a single sunny day can nearly or fully refill (1.7–2.2 sun-days). 2,000 mAh cells (eneloop, Brightown) need 3+ sun-days, so in short winter days they mostly sit partly charged. By cost per Wh from the makers' own stores, the Tenergy Solla Premium 1300 20-pack ($0.88/Wh) and the Solla 1000 24-pack ($0.90/Wh) beat the 12-packs. EBL's own store, at $3.75 a cell for a 4-pack, is the poorest value. So for most lights the pick is the Solla 1000 (24-pack) or the Solla Premium 1300 (20-pack), not a 2,000 mAh cell.
